mainTopic: Following a majority for lineage: the double-majority rule, the principle that anything קבוע counts as half and half, and רב's ruling about רבי יוסי
overview: The גמרא says the earlier incident happened at the wagons of ציפורי. It explains, using רבי אמי and רבי ינאי, that a woman is fit for כהונה only when both the city and a passing group are mostly of proper lineage. If one man came out of the city alone, the child is a שתוקי. A teaching that we follow the city's majority and not the group's is challenged as backwards. It is reread to mean that two majorities are needed. Neither one alone is enough, because a man whom she went to inside the city is קבוע, and קבוע counts as half and half. The meat-store ברייתא seems to show that one majority is enough. The answer is that חכמים set a higher standard for יוחסין. The גמרא then finds רבי זירא's source that קבוע counts as half and half even when this leads to leniency. It brings the case of nine שרצים and one frog, and the Torah source is the פסוק 'וארב לו' about a stone thrown into a group. Finally, two reports of רב disagree about whether the הלכה follows רבי יוסי. רבי ירמיה begins a challenge from a משנה that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The incident happened at the wagons of ציפורי
steps.stepSummary: The incident discussed just before happened among the wagons of ציפורי. The ruling there follows רבי אמי, who limits it to when a group of proper-lineage people was passing by.
steps.simpleTranslation: The incident took place among the wagons of ציפורי. This fits רבי אמי, who said the ruling only applies when a group of people with proper lineage was passing through there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the place where the earlier incident happened and ties the ruling to רבי אמי's condition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אמי adds a limit: the woman is only judged fit when a group of proper-lineage people was passing through. So both the people of the place and the passing group are mostly proper, and the man is assumed to be one of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Wagons; the caravans of traders passing through
ציפורי, a city in the Galil
A group or caravan of travelers
People of proper, unflawed lineage

phrases.english: The incident happened among the wagons of Tzippori,
and it is in line with Rabbi Ami.
As Rabbi Ami said:
And that is only when there was a group
of people of proper lineage
passing through there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens this section by locating the earlier incident.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lenient ruling applies only when a group of proper-lineage people was passing through.

steps.title: רבי ינאי: relations in the wagons leave her fit for כהונה
steps.stepSummary: The ruling also fits רבי ינאי, who said a woman with relations 'in the wagons' stays fit to marry a כהן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It also fits רבי ינאי, who said: a woman who had relations in the wagons is fit for כהונה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second אמורא whose ruling matches the incident at the wagons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ינאי gives the general rule: when relations happen 'in the wagons,' we assume the man was proper, so she may marry a כהן. His odd wording, 'in the wagons,' is what the next step questions.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who had relations
Fit to marry a כהן

phrases.english: And it is in line with Rabbi Yannai.
As Rabbi Yannai said:
A woman who had relations in the wagons
is fit for the priesthood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second אמורא whose ruling matches the incident.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who had relations 'in the wagons' is fit for כהונה.

steps.title: Could it really have happened in the wagons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how anyone could think the relations took place right in the wagons, in a crowded public place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can it enter your mind that it was 'in the wagons'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי ינאי's wording, setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken literally, 'in the wagons' means in the middle of the busy market, which makes no sense. So the wording must mean something else.

keyTerms.meaning: Would it enter your mind? (this cannot be meant literally)

phrases.english: In the wagons — can that enter your mind?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the literal wording of רבי ינאי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'נבעלת בקרונות' in רבי ינאי's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Relations would not happen inside the crowded wagons area, so the literal reading cannot be right.

steps.title: It means at the time the wagons pass
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי means relations that happened while the wagons were passing through; in that case she is fit for כהונה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: a woman who had relations at the time of the wagons is fit for כהונה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by rereading 'in the wagons' as 'at the time of the wagons.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is about timing, not place. When the caravan of proper people is passing, the man could be from them or from the city, and both groups are mostly proper.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; introduces the corrected reading
At the time of

phrases.english: Rather, a woman who had relations at the time of the wagons
is fit for the priesthood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge on the wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'In the wagons' means the place where it happened.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'In the wagons' means the time when the wagons were passing.

steps.title: If one man left ציפורי, the child is a שתוקי
steps.stepSummary: If a single man came out of ציפורי itself and had relations with her, the child is a שתוקי.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if one man left ציפורי and had relations, the child is a שתוקי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to רבי ינאי's lenient ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lenient ruling works because a passing group was there. When we know the man came out of the city, we do not use that leniency, and the child's status is left in doubt as a שתוקי.

keyTerms.meaning: Separated from, came out of
A child whose father is unknown; his lineage is in doubt

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 4. Step 4 is when the wagons are passing; here one man clearly came out of the city itself, so the result is stricter.

phrases.english: But if one man left Tzippori and had relations —
the child is a shetuki.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the lenient ruling just explained.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When one man came out of the city itself, the child is a שתוקי.

steps.title: רב דימי's report: follow the city's majority, not the group's
steps.stepSummary: A similar teaching: when רב דימי came, he reported in the name of זעירי and רבי חנינא that we follow the majority of the city, not the majority of a passing group.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what was said when רב דימי came: זעירי said in the name of רבי חנינא (and some say זעירי said in the name of רבי חנינא): we go after the majority of the city, and not after the majority of the passing group.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a similar teaching about which majority counts, the city's or the passing group's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two majorities: the people living in the city and the people traveling through. This teaching says the city's majority decides, not the group's. The next step will attack this.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this; brings a similar teaching
And some say; another version of who said it
Majority
We go after, we follow

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּכִי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי,
phrases.english: Like this: when Rav Dimi came,
he said that Ze'eiri said that Rabbi Ḥanina said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ, אָמַר זְעֵירִי אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: and some say: Ze'eiri said that Rabbi Ḥanina said:
We follow the majority of the city,
and we do not follow the majority of the group.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּכִי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a similar teaching about city majority versus group majority.
steps.raayaObject: Deciding which majority counts, the city's or the passing group's.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב דימי's report of זעירי and רבי חנינא: follow the city's majority, not the group's.

steps.title: The opposite makes sense: moving versus fixed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that this is backwards. The group is moving, which is where we follow the majority. The city people are fixed in place, which is where we do not simply follow the majority.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just the opposite! These people of the group are moving, and these people of the city are fixed and standing in place!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב דימי's rule as backwards. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When people are moving, we say whoever came out came from the majority, so we follow the majority. When people are fixed in place, the doubt is treated as if it were 50/50, even if most are proper. So the group, not the city, should be the one that decides.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary! It should be the other way
Moving, not settled in one place
Fixed and standing in one place (a קבוע)

steps.whyThisMatters: The difference between moving people and fixed people is a basic rule for using a majority, and it shows up across ש"ס.

phrases.english: On the contrary!
phrases.notes: Literally 'towards where?', meaning 'you have it backwards.'

phrases.english: These are moving,
and these are fixed and standing in place!
phrases.notes: 'These' means the people living in the city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule from רב דימי just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that we follow the city's majority and not the group's majority.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Normally we follow the majority when people are moving, and treat it as 50/50 when people are fixed. So the moving group should decide, not the fixed city.

steps.title: Two majorities are needed: the city and the passing group
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the teaching: we follow the majority of the city only when the passing group also has a fit majority. Neither majority alone is enough, because of a decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: we follow the majority of the city, but only when the majority of the passing group agrees with it. We do not follow the city's majority alone, and we do not follow the group's majority alone. Why not the group alone? חכמים made a decree about the group's majority because of the city's majority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the backwards-sounding teaching from step 7 by reading it a new way: you need a majority in both places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 asked how we could follow the fixed city and not the moving group. The new reading says we follow neither one alone; we need both majorities to point the same way. The group's majority alone is not enough because people could mix it up with the city's majority, which really cannot be relied on.

keyTerms.meaning: The majority of the passing group of travelers
Alone, by itself
A protective decree made by חכמים
Because of, so it won't be confused with

steps.confusionAlert: The 'decree' is not about the city's majority. It says we can't rely on the group's majority alone, because people might confuse it with the city's majority.

phrases.english: Rather: one follows the majority of the city,
phrases.notes: The גמרא is rereading the teaching quoted in step 6.

phrases.english: but only when there is a majority of the group along with it,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין הוֹלְכִין אַחַר רוֹב הָעִיר גְּרֵידְתָּא,
phrases.english: but one does not follow the majority of the city alone,
nor the majority of the group alone.
What is the reason?

phrases.aramaic: גְּזֵרָה רוֹב סִיעָה אַטּוּ רוֹב הָעִיר.
phrases.english: A decree about the majority of the group because of the majority of the city.
phrases.notes: We may not rely on the group's majority alone, so that people won't rely on the city's majority alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: הוֹלְכִין אַחַר רוֹב הָעִיר, וְהוּא דְּאִיכָּא רוֹב סִיעָה בַּהֲדַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 7 by rereading the teaching.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the earlier teaching so that it needs a double majority
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We follow the city's majority instead of the group's majority, which sounds backwards.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both majorities must agree. Neither one alone is enough, because of a decree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For lineage, we follow the majority only when the city and the passing group both have a fit majority.

steps.title: Sometimes the city's majority should also work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a decree is needed. If a city man went out to her, he left his fixed place, so the city's majority should count.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the city's majority also works sometimes: if the men go out to her, then whoever separated from the group separated from the majority!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the decree from step 8. Even the city's majority can be relied on in a normal case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that anything that leaves its group is judged by the group's majority. If a city man came out to her, he 'separated' from the city. So the city's majority should be fine, and there seems to be no reason for a decree.

keyTerms.meaning: Whatever separates from a group is treated as coming from its majority
To her, toward her

phrases.english: But the majority of the city also works,
if they go out to her:
whatever separates, separates from the majority!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרוֹב הָעִיר נָמֵי, אִי דְּקָא אָזְלִי אִינְהוּ לְגַבַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason for the decree given in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the city's majority can't be relied on, which is the basis of the decree
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: When the man comes out of the city, the rule of כל דפריש applies. So the city's majority should be valid, and no decree is needed.

steps.title: The decree is for when she went into the city
steps.stepSummary: The decree is needed for the case where she went into the city. Then the man is in his fixed place, and קבוע counts as half and half.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only where she went to them, so the man is 'fixed', and רבי זירא said: anything fixed is treated like half and half.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the decree is about the case where the woman went into the city to the men.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When she goes to them, the man never left his place, so he is קבוע. רבי זירא teaches that a doubt about something קבוע is treated as an even fifty-fifty doubt, and the majority does not decide it. In that case the city's majority really does not work, so the decree is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)
Fixed in its place
Like half and half, an even doubt

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule of קבוע (anything fixed counts as half and half) is a basic tool for doubts all across ש״ס.

phrases.english: It is needed only
where she goes to them,
so that he counts as fixed,
and רבי זירא said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל קָבוּעַ כְּמֶחֱצָה עַל מֶחֱצָה דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: anything fixed is considered like half and half.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּקָא אָזְלָא אִיהִי לְגַבַּיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 9 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the decree to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The city's majority always works, so no decree is needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: When she went into the city, the man is קבוע and the majority doesn't count. The decree exists because of that case.
steps.whatToRemember: For lineage we need two majorities. One alone isn't trusted, because in the city case the man may be קבוע, and קבוע counts as half and half.

steps.title: The meat stores show one majority is enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether we really need two majorities. A ברייתא about meat stores follows one simple majority for meat found in the street.
steps.simpleTranslation: And do we really need two majorities? But a ברייתא teaches: there are nine stores that all sell slaughtered meat and one that sells נבלה meat. If someone bought from one of them and doesn't know which, the doubt is forbidden. But if meat is found in the street, follow the majority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the double-majority rule of step 8 using a ברייתא about kosher meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of buying in a store is like 'she went to them': the store is קבוע, so it is half and half and the meat is forbidden. But meat found in the street has 'separated', and there one majority of stores is enough. So why does lineage need two majorities?

keyTerms.meaning: Two majorities
Stores
Meat from a properly slaughtered animal
Meat from an animal not properly slaughtered, which is forbidden
Something found, here meat found in the street

phrases.english: And do we need two majorities?
But it is taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: תֵּשַׁע חֲנוּיוֹת כּוּלָּן מוֹכְרוֹת בְּשַׂר שְׁחוּטָה,
phrases.english: nine stores, all of which sell slaughtered meat,
and one sells נבלה meat,
and he bought from one of them

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ מֵאֵי זֶה מֵהֶן לָקַח —
phrases.english: and he does not know which of them he bought from:
in this doubt, the meat is forbidden.
phrases.notes: He bought it right at the store, so it is a 'fixed' case, like step 10.

phrases.english: And with meat that was found, follow the majority.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the double-majority requirement set in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that two majorities are needed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא follows a single majority for found meat. That shows one majority is enough, without a decree to require two.

steps.title: The open-gates answer is rejected
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the meat case also has two majorities, since the city gates are open. It rejects this, because רבי זירא said the rule holds even when the gates are locked.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the ברייתא means the city gates are not locked, so a majority of kosher meat also comes from the outside world, giving two majorities: but רבי זירא said the rule holds even when the city gates are locked!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries an answer: the meat case really has two majorities too. Then it knocks that answer down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggested answer says that with open gates, meat could come from outside, where most meat is kosher. That would add a second majority. But רבי זירא said we follow the majority even with locked gates, so the meat case really has only one majority, and the question comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (a suggested answer)
The city gates are locked
From the outside world

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי תֵּימָא בְּשֶׁאֵין דַּלְתוֹת מְדִינָה נְעוּלוֹת,
phrases.english: And if you would say: where the city gates are not locked,
so that a majority comes to it from the outside world,
phrases.notes: Meaning most meat outside the city is also kosher, so that would be a second majority.

phrases.english: but רבי זירא said:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁדַּלְתוֹת מְדִינָה נְעוּלוֹת!
phrases.english: even if the city gates are locked!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא בְּשֶׁאֵין דַּלְתוֹת מְדִינָה נְעוּלוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests an answer to step 11 and rejects it right away.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggested answer that the meat case also has two majorities
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי זירא rules that we follow the majority even with locked gates, so the meat case has only one majority.

steps.title: A higher standard for lineage
steps.stepSummary: The answer: חכמים set a stricter standard for יוחסין, so two majorities are needed there. For meat, one is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: They made a higher standard for lineage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final answer: lineage is treated more strictly than kosher meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the letter of the law, one majority is enough, as the meat case shows. For family lineage, חכמים added extra strictness and required two majorities. So the meat ברייתא does not contradict the double-majority rule.

keyTerms.meaning: An extra, higher standard of strictness
Family lineage, purity of descent

steps.whatToRemember: One majority is normally enough, as with found meat. For יוחסין, חכמים required two majorities as a מעלה, and anything קבוע counts as half and half.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why lineage is held to a stricter standard than other areas of הלכה, like kosher meat.

phrases.english: They made a higher standard for lineage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the real answer to the קשיא of step 11 after step 12's answer was rejected.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Telling the cases apart: a stricter standard for lineage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since one majority is enough for meat, it should be enough for lineage too.
steps.terutzMaskana: Lineage needs two majorities because חכמים set a higher standard. Meat needs only one.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The double-majority rule is a special strictness for יוחסין, not the general rule for majorities.

steps.title: Anything fixed in place counts as half and half
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to quote רבי זירא's rule on its own: anything קבוע counts as half and half, whether that leads to a lenient or a strict result.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the rule itself. רבי זירא said: anything that is fixed in its place is treated like a half-and-half doubt, whether that ends up lenient or strict.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to look closely at רבי זירא's rule, which was used in the earlier steps. This sets up the next question: where does he learn it from?
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the doubt comes from something still in its fixed place, we do not follow the majority. Instead we treat the case as an even 50/50 doubt. רבי זירא adds that this works both ways: sometimes it makes the law stricter and sometimes more lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The thing itself.' The גמרא is going back to study a statement it quoted earlier.
Fixed. The doubt comes from an item that is still in its fixed place.
Like half and half: an evenly balanced doubt, where we do not follow the majority.
Toward leniency.
Toward stringency.

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'both for leniency and for stringency' are the key to the rest of this section. The גמרא will reject any source that only shows the strict side.

phrases.english: The matter itself: Rabbi Zeira said:
Anything fixed in its place
is considered like half and half,
whether for leniency or for stringency.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to examine on its own the rule of רבי זירא that was used earlier in the sugya.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anything קבוע is treated as an evenly balanced doubt, and this applies whether the result is lenient or strict.

steps.title: Where does this rule come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what source רבי זירא has for his rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where does רבי זירא know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רבי זירא's source. This opens a search, and the next steps will try out possible sources one after another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source has to prove the whole rule, including the claim that it applies 'even for leniency.' This is why the suggestions that follow will be tested on that point.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he know it? A request for a source.
This (rule).

phrases.english: From where does Rabbi Zeira know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which earlier source shows that anything קבוע is half and half, both leniently and strictly.

steps.title: First try: the nine stores
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the case of nine kosher stores and one store selling נבילה. Meat bought from a store, when we don't know which one, is forbidden. Meat found in the street follows the majority.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say he learns it from the case of nine stores that all sell properly slaughtered meat and one store that sells נבילה meat: if someone bought from one of them and doesn't know which one, the doubtful meat is forbidden. But meat found in the street follows the majority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a first possible source: the meat-store case. Here meat bought straight from a store, which is קבוע, is treated as a doubt and forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most stores are kosher, yet meat bought straight from a store is forbidden. That shows a קבוע case is not decided by the majority. Meat found in the street, which has left its fixed place, does follow the majority.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say. This brings in a suggestion that will be tested.
Meat from an animal that was properly slaughtered (kosher).
An animal that died without proper slaughter. Its meat is forbidden.
The found item: meat found away from the stores.
Follow the majority.

phrases.english: If you say from nine stores,
all of which sell slaughtered meat,
and one sells meat of a carcass,
and he bought from one of them
and he does not know from which of them he bought,
his doubtful meat is forbidden,
and with found meat
follow the majority;
phrases.notes: This is the same meat-store ברייתא the גמרא brought in step 11.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to the question about the source.
steps.raayaObject: רבי זירא's rule that anything קבוע is half and half.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of nine kosher stores and one נבילה store.

steps.title: The stores case only shows the strict side
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the stores source, because there the half-and-half rule only makes things stricter.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it works out strictly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the first suggestion. That case only proves the strict half of רבי זירא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Following the majority would have made the meat kosher. Treating it as half and half made it forbidden, which is stricter. But רבי זירא also said the rule applies 'for leniency,' and this case cannot prove that part.

keyTerms.meaning: There, meaning in that case.
Majority.

phrases.english: There it is for stringency!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the source offered in step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the stores case as a full source for רבי זירא's rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It shows only that קבוע makes things stricter, not that it can also make them more lenient.

steps.title: Second try: nine frogs and one שרץ
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a case of nine frogs and one שרץ. Someone touched one of them and doesn't know which, and he is טמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he learns it from the case of nine frogs with one שרץ among them. Someone touched one of them and doesn't know which one he touched. His doubt is טמא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second possible source, from the laws of טומאה. Here too the majority is not followed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most of the creatures are frogs, which do not make a person טמא. Even so, the person who touched one is טמא. The majority was ignored and the case was treated as a doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. Brings in a new suggestion after the last one was rejected.
Frog. Touching one does not make a person טמא.
A creeping creature whose dead body makes a person טמא.
Ritually impure.

phrases.english: Rather, from nine frogs
and one creeping creature among them,
and he touched one of them,
and he does not know which of them he touched,
his doubt is impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 17 rejected the stores source, this offers a different one.
steps.raayaObject: רבי זירא's rule that anything קבוע is half and half.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of nine frogs and one שרץ.

steps.title: The frogs case is also only strict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the frogs source too, because there as well the half-and-half rule only makes things stricter.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too it works out strictly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the second suggestion for the same reason as the first. Again, only the strict side of the rule is shown.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Following the majority of frogs would have made the person טהור. Treating the case as half and half made him טמא, which is stricter. We still need a case where the rule leads to leniency.

keyTerms.meaning: Also, too.

phrases.english: There too it is for stringency!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the source offered in step 18 for the same reason as step 17.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the frogs case as a full source for רבי זירא's rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It shows only the strict result, not the lenient one.

steps.title: The real source: nine שרצים and one frog
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the reverse case: nine שרצים and one frog. In a private domain he is טמא, but in רשות הרבים he is טהור, even though most of the creatures would make him טמא. This shows the lenient side of the rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he learns it from the case of nine שרצים with one frog among them. Someone touched one of them and doesn't know which one he touched. In a private domain, his doubt is טמא. In a public domain, his doubt is טהור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finally finds a case where treating something קבוע as half and half leads to a lenient result. This is the source for רבי זירא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here most of the creatures are שרצים, so following the majority would make the person טמא. But since the creatures are קבוע, the case counts as an even doubt. A doubt about טומאה in רשות הרבים is ruled טהור, so the person is טהור. This proves the rule works 'for leniency' too.

keyTerms.meaning: A private domain. Doubts about טומאה there are ruled impure.
A public domain. Doubts about טומאה there are ruled pure.
Ritually pure.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא's source is the public-domain case of nine שרצים and one frog. The majority points to טמא, but because the creatures are קבוע the case counts as an even doubt, and the person is טהור. So קבוע can lead to a lenient result as well as a strict one.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for the proof in the private-domain ruling. There the person is טמא either way. The proof comes only from the public-domain ruling, where he is טהור against the majority.
steps.whyThisMatters: This completes the proof for both sides of רבי זירא's rule. It shows that קבוע is a real rule of doubt that sets the majority aside, not just an extra stringency.

phrases.english: Rather, from nine creeping creatures
and one frog among them,
and he touched one of them,
and he does not know which of them he touched.
In a private domain, his doubt is impure.
In a public domain, his doubt is pure.
phrases.notes: Most of the creatures here are שרצים, yet he is pure. That lenient result is the proof the גמרא was looking for.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִתִּשְׁעָה שְׁרָצִים וּצְפַרְדֵּעַ אֶחָד בֵּינֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After two sources were rejected for showing only the strict side, this brings a case that shows the lenient side.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי זירא learns his rule from the case of nine שרצים and one frog in רשות הרבים. There the case is treated as an even doubt and ruled טהור, even though most of the creatures would make him טמא.

steps.title: What is the Torah source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source in the Torah itself for the rule that קבוע is treated as half-and-half, even when that leads to leniency.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we learn this from the Torah?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has already shown this rule from a ברייתא, and now asks where the Torah itself teaches it. This question sets up the next move, where a פסוק will be brought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 showed from the frogs case that קבוע can make things lenient. Now the גמרא wants a source from the Torah itself, not just a rabbinic teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: From the Torah itself
From where do we know this?

phrases.english: And from the Torah, from where do we know it?
phrases.notes: 'It' means the rule that something fixed in its place counts as half-and-half, even when that makes things more lenient.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the frogs case, the גמרא looks for a Torah-level source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A Torah source showing that קבוע is treated as half-and-half even when this leads to leniency.

steps.title: The verse about lying in wait
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'and he lies in wait for him and rises against him' teaches that a killer is liable only if he aimed at that specific person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And he lies in wait for him and rises up against him.' This means he is liable only when he intended to kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a פסוק about a murderer. The פסוק shows that the killer must have aimed at the victim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'for him' are read as 'for him specifically.' This reading means that someone who meant to kill one person and killed another is exempt. This is the starting point, and the next steps will show how it connects to קבוע.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק says
And he lies in wait for him
That he intends to kill him specifically

phrases.english: The verse says: "And he lies in wait for him and rises up against him,"
meaning, he is not liable until he intends to kill him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a Torah source by quoting a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'וארב לו' teaches that liability for murder requires intent toward the specific victim.

steps.title: How do the רבנן use the verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the רבנן learn from this פסוק, since they hold that someone who aimed at one person and killed another is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, what do they learn from it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the רבנן do with this פסוק, since they do not use it to exempt someone who killed the wrong person. This sets up the answer that will give the real source for קבוע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reading in step 22 belongs to one view. The רבנן disagree with it, so the פסוק must teach them something else.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, here the view that disagrees with the reading above

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: He means: what do the רבנן learn from this פסוק, since they don't exempt someone who killed a different person than he aimed at?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the opposing view reads the same פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from 'ואָרַב לוֹ'.

steps.title: Excluding a stone thrown into a group
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי says the פסוק exempts someone who throws a stone into a group of people.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ינאי says: the פסוק comes to exclude someone who throws a stone into a group.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is that, according to the רבנן, the פסוק exempts a person who throws a stone into a group without aiming at anyone specific.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the thrower did not aim at any one person, he is exempt. The next steps will ask what this group looks like, and that is where קבוע comes in.

keyTerms.meaning: The school of רבי ינאי
To exclude
One who throws a stone into a group

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:
To exclude one who throws a stone into a group.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers how the רבנן use the פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to the רבנן, the פסוק exempts one who throws a stone into a group.

steps.title: Why would we need a verse for this case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the group looks like. If most are gentiles, majority already exempts him. If it is half-and-half, ספק נפשות להקל already exempts him.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If there are nine gentiles and one Jew among them, we already know he is exempt because most are gentiles. And if it is half-and-half, we are lenient in a doubt about a life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the need for the פסוק. In both simple versions of the case, the thrower is already exempt without it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If most of the group are gentiles, the majority rule already exempts him. If the group is evenly split, the rule ספק נפשות להקל already exempts him. So the גמרא asks what the פסוק is adding.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case?
He could learn it anyway from a different reason
Half and half
When there is a doubt in a case of life and death, we are lenient

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If we say that there are nine gentiles
and one Jew among them,
let him learn it from the fact that the majority are gentiles.
Alternatively, if it is half and half,
in a doubt about life, we are lenient.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what case the exemption from step 24 is talking about, and attacks the need for the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the פסוק to exempt one who throws a stone into a group.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both a gentile majority and an even split already lead to an exemption through other rules, so the פסוק would teach nothing new.

steps.title: Nine Jews and one fixed gentile
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is needed for nine Jews and one gentile. The gentile is קבוע, and anything קבוע counts as half-and-half, so the thrower is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where there are nine Jews and one gentile among them. The gentile is fixed in place, and anything fixed counts as half-and-half.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק is about a group with mostly Jews. Following the majority would make the thrower liable, but because the gentile is קבוע, the case counts as half-and-half and he is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Following the majority would make him liable. The פסוק shows that קבוע turns this into half-and-half, and then ספק נפשות להקל exempts him. This is the Torah source we wanted: קבוע counts as half-and-half even when the result is lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed only for this case
Fixed in its place, not separated from the group
It counts like half-and-half

steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק 'ואָרַב לוֹ' (as the רבנן read it) is the Torah source that קבוע counts as half-and-half, even when this leads to a leniency like exemption from the death penalty.
steps.confusionAlert: We do not follow the majority of nine Jews here. Because the gentile is קבוע, the majority is ignored and the case becomes an even 50-50 doubt.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answers step 21. It shows from the Torah that קבוע works in both directions, which is exactly רבי זירא's point.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where there are nine Jews
and one gentile among them,
so the gentile is fixed,
and anything fixed
is considered like half and half.
phrases.notes: Once it counts as half-and-half, the rule from the last step applies: in a doubt about a life, we are lenient.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by naming a case where only קבוע produces the exemption.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the case is limited to a Jewish majority with one fixed gentile.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seemed unnecessary, since majority or ספק נפשות would already exempt him.
steps.terutzMaskana: With nine Jews and one fixed gentile, majority would make him liable. Only the rule of קבוע makes it half-and-half, which leads to the exemption.

steps.title: First report: the הלכה follows רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אשי reports that רב ruled the הלכה follows רבי יוסי in the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב חייא בר אשי said in the name of רב: the הלכה follows רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic and brings a ruling of רב about רבי יוסי's story in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יוסי told of a girl who was violated, and she was allowed to marry a כהן based on the majority of the town. According to this report, רב rules that this is the הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a statement of the אמוראים)
The final ruling follows

phrases.aramaic: אִיתְּמַר, רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: It was stated: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi said that Rav said:
The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.
phrases.notes: This goes back to רבי יוסי's story in the משנה about the girl who was allowed to marry a כהן.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר, רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the קבוע discussion and goes back to the משנה's case about family lineage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows רבי יוסי, and the girl may marry a כהן.

steps.title: Second report: it was a one-time ruling
steps.stepSummary: רב חנן בר רבא reports that רב said רבי יוסי's case was only a ruling for that specific time.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חנן בר רבא said in the name of רב: it was a ruling for that time only.
steps.whatsHappening: A second student reports רב differently. He says the ruling in רבי יוסי's story was a special ruling for that moment only, not the normal הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the same case is treated as a one-time exception. In normal cases of family lineage, more than one majority is needed. So the two reports of רב disagree about whether the story sets the הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: A ruling for that time only, because of special circumstances

steps.whatToRemember: There are two reports of רב: one says the הלכה follows רבי יוסי, and the other says that story was only a one-time ruling.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חָנָן בַּר רָבָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: And Rav Ḥanan bar Rava said that Rav said:
It was a provisional ruling for that time.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב חָנָן בַּר רָבָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, conflicting report of רב's view on the same case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוסי's case was a one-time ruling and does not set the normal הלכה.

steps.title: Do lineage cases really need two majorities?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה challenges the ruling that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי, and introduces a משנה as his source.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה objected: For lineage, don't we need two majorities? But didn't we learn in a משנה:
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה raises a challenge against the ruling that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי. This line only sets up his challenge. The משנה he relies on is quoted at the start of the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ruled that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי, which seems to mean that one majority is enough to allow marriage into כהונה. רבי ירמיה is surprised by this. He holds that lineage questions should need two majorities, and he is about to bring a משנה to show it.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection, usually from an earlier source like a משנה or ברייתא
Lineage, meaning family status that matters for marriage, for example into כהונה
Two majorities
But didn't we learn in a משנה? This introduces a source used as proof

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not answer anything. It only opens the challenge. The actual proof comes from the משנה quoted on the next amud.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya raised an objection:
And for lineage, don't we require two majorities?
phrases.notes: He is surprised. רב's ruling for רבי יוסי seems to rely on just one majority.

phrases.english: But didn't we learn in a משנה:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling, reported by רב חייא בר אשי in step 27, that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the הלכה follows רבי יוסי, which seems to rely on only one majority for lineage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Lineage should need two majorities, so ruling like רבי יוסי with just one majority seems wrong. A משנה is about to be brought as the source.
